Taxonomic classification of animal species follows the Linnaean hierarchical system (Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species), though contemporary systematics increasingly relies on phylogenetic (cladistic) methods that group organisms by shared derived characteristics rather than overall morphological similarity. The distinction matters: convergent evolution can produce superficially similar forms (e.g., the wings of bats and birds) that do not reflect close evolutionary relationship.

Metabolic rate scales with body mass according to Kleiber's law, which states that basal metabolic rate is proportional to body mass raised to the three-quarter power (M^0.75). This sublinear relationship means that larger animals are more metabolically efficient per unit mass. A 3-gram shrew, for instance, must consume roughly 1.5 times its body weight in food daily, whereas a 5,000-kilogram elephant requires food equivalent to only 1.5 to 2 percent of its body weight.

Animal communication systems exhibit considerable sophistication. Vervet monkeys produce acoustically distinct alarm calls for eagles, snakes, and leopards (each eliciting a different and contextually appropriate evasive response). Whether such systems constitute "language" depends on definitional criteria, but they demonstrably encode referential information, challenging earlier assumptions that symbolic communication is exclusively a human capacity.
